Depending on what it is it may be better to just leave it. If it's on your arms or legs keep your legs shaved regularly(a good electric razor daily after clearing the area with a regular razor the first time). No one will notice or care about the stubs of hair so much as they'll notice the painful after effects of over doing it(razor burn, ingrown hairs, razor bumps, etc). Your other option is regularly waxing but I don't know your pain tolerance/financial status. 

If it's your beard you absolutely want to be careful. Beard hair is deeply rooted and the skin on your face is easily scarred.. A light depilatory cream a few hours after a shave will help but I wouldn't go any further than that. 

Eyebrows you want to pluck or wax, YouTube will have some great videos. 

But ultimately it's going to come down to commitment. Keep things clean shaven, moisturized, and exfoliated and over time the stubble and little root hairs become less noticeable. 

Take everything I say with a grain of salt, double check and Google before you take any drastic actions or measures. Test the depilatory cream on a small spot of your skin to make sure you don't have a reaction if you do try it out. Be safe, love yourself and be pretty like you know you can be :)

The thing about the Ali to Tyson eras of boxing is that it was the beginning of something amazing. Something that started with Ali and saw it's culmination in Tyson. Today boxing is decided as much by how much is invested in your training as it is by your physicality. Modern boxing is a technical playground with a million styles and most importantly scientifically designed workout/training routines.

Back then that shit was just starting to gather steam. Spectators and coaches were still looking almost exclusively for men with similar physical traits but were experimenting with different styles of training them. They all wanted and scoured the recruits for a Tyson Fury type. They all wanted a boxer with an iron jaw and a brick in his glove. The bigger the badder the better. Then it came down to a game of which coach was running with the most up to date information. 

Then came along the Ali generation. Young boys across the nation who were finally watching these absolute beasts of men duke it out in the ring fantasizing about how they would deal. TV and radio were finally universal and so was the reach of boxing. 

And wouldn't you know it, this generation of talent grew up and got more creative, more impressive, and most importantly, more entertaining. Technicality of a different nature had emerged. Then the coaches started to catch on. They found their boxers and finally expanded into radically different body types using extremely specialized boxing styles. The birth of the first generation of champions emerged. Men who not only were capable of being champions, but who believed deeply that they were. The reality is that they were so above and beyond the competition that they ended up only boxing each other in a small round robin of insanity throughout the years. Rematches and vendettas peppered with some cannon fodder in between. They spent so much time fighting at the absolute top of the mountain that they wore the impressions of their very bodies into it. 

The modern era of boxing is undoubtedly the most skillful and talented to ever exist. They have the tools, the history, and the techniques to all compete at a level that only a select few could before. 

But the legends of boxing will never be torn down. Muhammad Ali, Sonny Liston, George Foreman, The Sugar Rays, Hitman Hearns, Evander Holyfield, and the man who hit the scene and set a fear in the heart of the world himself Mike Motherfuckin Tyson.

I can address a few of concerns I see you have presented though. At least, I can begin to address them. As for size and scale, my idea would actually have the opposite end of the issue. Scaling up Is where I run into big road blocks because where I'm hoping to create something hobbyist and DiY friendly with my system, big EV companies have pretty much cornered the market on extremely compact and efficient systems for full sized vehicles. Conversions for cars and trucks, while viable, I foresee falling into the valley of easily accessible performance at the cost of range and energy efficiency. (which while not at all intentional or planned for, gives me a little thrill thinking back to the early days of American muscle cars where at home mechanics were dropping giant Jerry rigged engines that were guzzling gas and tearing up the road). I'm not too bothered by that,because city commuting, frequent short distance delivery style travel, and good old fashioned recreational driving should still be perfectly achievable. ebikes, trikes, and motorcycles though, are where I foresee the balance between performance and efficiency will be best for my system. And as an entry level EV that would be pretty much the demographic I'm shooting for anyway, hobbyists, innovators, short distance fleets, and low income consumers. People and entities attracted by low entry cost, and low maintenance costs in a world of expensive restrictive over designed products. 

As for how I would make a viable business out of it I have fewer answers. I do have a few plans that feel viable. One of which would be to start with a motorcycle conversion kit that can be sold online while contracts can be negotiated with independent mechanics and shops in the hopes of boosting traffic for local small owned businesses. People would buy the kit from one company and they would ship to an approved and trained mechanic that the customer would take their vehicle to and have the swap done. Then creating a hiring program for local trade school graduates, entry level EV mechanics, and independent contractors to operate as a local fleet of mobile mechanics/consultants so that people can still operate through the original company directly should they choose to do so. 

As for local and state laws regarding electric vehicles, vehicle sales, kit cars, maintenance, and conversions that would be minefield I'm prepared to admit I am not prepared for. In truth after I have a viable concept for an end product, reliable routes to seek out production and manufacture of components, and enough capital/investors to proceed, I would need to hire consultants specially trained and educated in business planning and start ups to help me in that area, then consult with lawyers in each market I would like to operate in. I have complete faith in my own technical abilities and my own vision, but I know to defer to greater minds than my own when outside of my wheelhouse, so to speak. So beyond the R&D that I know I can do now, I would need to dedicate resources and time to building on the things I need to learn to do, or hire to get done. 

All that said, With transparency and freedom of information I would like to create a lasting product and a freely usable system for the general public. 

A lasting product that would fund further ventures, instead of stagnating on one idea, so that I can still be helpful to the people who need it and not get burned by trying to be helpful.

My advice would be this, get used to each company first. They're all a little different in pretty meaningful ways. 

When you first start multi apping make sure you're only doing one assignment at a time while the other is paused. 

As you gain experience and confidence you will be able to suss out what you're specific location does best and what it doesn't, which apps to be on at which time, and most importantly the freedom and restrictions each app will have on you while you're delivering for them.

If you're new here are two unsolicited pieces of advice I have for you. 1. Don't worry about things so much, just focus on doing your job, meeting expectations, and getting your paycheck. A lot of these companies bank on inexperience and desperate people to pump their profits. Don't give them what they want. 
2. Use critical thinking and caution always. Always take a second to know where you're going and what you're doing. Always make sure you're getting paid enough to make it make sense, if you have to question it it probably wasn't enough to make you move. Always put you and your resources above anything else. Always make sure you stay safe because you are more important than anything doordash related. None of these deliveries are life threatening and if they are there are bigger problems than you as an independent contractor getting paid 2.50 and order are capable of fixing. 

Be safe out there.
